title: CHOOSE YOU THIS DAY—BECAUSE THE GOD YOU REFUSE TO CHOOSE MAY BE THE GOD YOU ARE ALREADY REPLACING
paragraphs:
CHOOSE YOU THIS DAY—BECAUSE THE GOD YOU REFUSE TO CHOOSE MAY BE THE GOD YOU ARE ALREADY REPLACING
Joshua’s final challenge was not written for people who openly hated God. It was spoken to people who had seen His miracles, received His promises, and still needed to decide who would truly own their hearts.
There comes a moment when God stops allowing the question to remain comfortably theoretical.
Not because His grace has run out.
Not because He has become impatient.
But because eventually every heart must confront what it has been avoiding:
Not who do you say you believe in.
Not what religion appears on your profile.
Not what Christian songs you know.
Not what Bible verses you repost.
Not what your parents taught you.
Not what you tell people when they ask whether you believe in God.
Joshua was an old man when he gathered Israel at Shechem.
He had watched frightened wanderers become a nation possessing cities they had not built and vineyards they had not planted.
He knew what God had done.
And perhaps that is precisely why his final challenge was so severe.
Joshua did not gather Israel merely to tell them how wonderful they were.
He reminded them of how faithful God had been.
The words still thunder across the centuries:
“Choose you this day whom ye will serve.”
But there is something in the Hebrew that deserves to be heard.
“Choose for yourselves today whom you will serve.”
And then comes Joshua’s unforgettable declaration:
“But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”
Joshua was not shopping for gods.
The question was whether Israel had.
Because you can live thousands of years after Joshua and still stand at Shechem.
Your Shechem may be your bedroom at two in the morning.
Your Shechem may be the browser history nobody knows about.
Your Shechem may be the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Anything can become an altar when it receives the surrender that belongs to God.
And that is what makes Joshua’s challenge uncomfortable.
Because belief that never reaches allegiance is not the kind of faith Scripture calls us toward.
Even demons recognize who God is.
So perhaps the frightening question is not whether you believe in Jesus.
Perhaps the question is what your belief has done to you.
Has it brought you to repentance?
Has Christ become King, or merely emergency assistance?
Do you want Jesus Himself—or mainly what you hope Jesus will give you?
And sometimes that difference only becomes visible when obedience becomes expensive.
Everyone loves surrender when surrender costs nothing.
Then Jesus touches the thing we secretly placed above Him.
And suddenly Christianity becomes painfully real.
The Hebrew word הַיּוֹם—hayom—means “the day,” commonly rendered here “today” or “this day.”
There is urgency in Joshua’s challenge.
Because delayed obedience has a dangerous way of disguising itself as future faithfulness.
“I’ll come back to God when life settles down.”
“I know this relationship is wrong, but…”
“I know God has been convicting me, but…”
One tiny word has buried countless convictions.
Joshua refuses to give Israel the luxury of endless postponement.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly why those words hurt.
You remember when you were closer to God.
You remember when prayer was not merely something you did when frightened.
You remember when Scripture could break you open.
You remember when sin bothered you before you learned how to negotiate with it.
That is usually how spiritual drift works.
Nobody wakes up one morning and announces:
“Today I will destroy my relationship with God.”
Eventually the thing that once made you tremble barely makes you uncomfortable.
You still know the Christian vocabulary.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
But inside, something feels frighteningly quiet.
That is where Joshua’s story becomes more than confrontation.
Because Joshua 24 is not merely Israel being commanded to remember what they should do for God.
It begins with what God had already done for them.
Again and again, God is the acting One.
God reminds Israel that their story began with His initiative.
Because biblical surrender is not an attempt to purchase God’s love.
It is the response of people who have encountered it.
And this is where Joshua points us toward something even greater than Joshua.
Jesus leads sinners into reconciliation with God.
Joshua confronted Israel with covenant loyalty.
Jesus came to rescue covenant breakers who could never save themselves.
But Jesus would eventually walk toward a cross carrying the consequences of humanity choosing everything except God.
This is the scandal of grace.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
The cross proves exactly how serious sin is.
But the cross also reveals how astonishing the love of God is.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.”
Not people who finally managed to clean themselves up.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
That word should destroy both pride and despair.
Pride cannot survive because salvation was never your achievement.
Despair cannot survive because your failure did not prevent Christ from coming for sinners.
“Fix yourself so Jesus might accept you.”
The Gospel is that the holy Son of God entered our ruined story, bore sin at the cross, rose bodily from the dead, and calls sinners to repent and believe.
Jesus does not merely improve the old story.
He gives the sinner a new one.
Maybe people still whisper your name beside your worst decision.
You smile in photographs while carrying a war behind your eyes.
You know exactly what you have been hiding.
And the enemy has spent years telling you:
“If people knew the real you, they would leave.”
Maybe that fear has even shaped the way you imagine God.
So you hide from Him too.
But where exactly are you going to hide from the One who already knows everything?
Jesus did not discover your history after inviting you to come.
He knew the nights you would cry.
He knew the promises you would break.
He knew how many times you would say, “Never again,” only to fall again.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
An invitation to come out of hiding.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you away from the thing that is destroying you.
The New Testament word commonly translated “repent” is μετανοέω—metanoeō—carrying the sense of changing one’s mind, turning in response to truth.
Jesus began His public proclamation with this summons:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.”
Not because your sin is small.
“Jesus paid too great a price to leave you chained to what He came to save you from.”
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?”
Grace is not a comfortable blanket thrown over rebellion.
Grace brings dead people to life.
And living people begin walking differently.
Sometimes with tears and setbacks and desperate prayers?
Because when Jesus becomes Lord, the direction of a life begins to change.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear tonight.
You do not need another inspirational quote.
“Choose you this day whom ye will serve.”
Maybe you have been standing between two worlds.
One foot toward the thing Jesus keeps asking you to release.
You want enough Christianity to calm your conscience but not enough surrender to disrupt your lifestyle.
Because God wounds our illusions in order to heal what is real.
Joshua told Israel something startling immediately after their confident promise to serve the LORD:
“You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God.”
At first that sounds almost contradictory.
Joshua tells them to choose God, they say they will, and Joshua warns them about the seriousness of what they have said.
Because covenant allegiance is not casual.
Israel could not treat Him as one option among many.
Christianity is not Jesus plus the idols we refuse to surrender.
Jesus plus whatever culture says matters more than Scripture.
Jesus plus whatever god I manufacture in my own image.
Christ does not apply for a position in your life.
The question is whether we bow.
And here the Gospel becomes even more precious.
Because if salvation depended upon the perfection of our choosing, none of us could stand.
Jesus did what Joshua could never do.
He did not merely command sinners from a distance.
Christian hope ultimately rests not in our ability to hold onto God tightly enough, but in the saving work of Christ received through faith.
That does not eliminate the call to choose.
It finally shows us where the power to follow comes from.
Not because following Jesus guarantees an easy life.
Some habits must be dragged into the light.
The cross was never marketed as comfortable.
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”
There is Joshua’s challenge again in another form.
When nobody is watching, choose again.
When obedience costs you, choose again.
When God feels silent, choose again.
When your prayers seem unanswered, choose again.
When you fall, repent, get back up, and choose again—not to earn salvation, but because the One who saved you is worthy.
And one day you may look backward and realize something extraordinary.
The thousands of small decisions to follow Jesus became a life.
A daughter broke a generational pattern.
A secret addiction lost its grip.
A household discovered what Joshua meant:
“As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”
Maybe your household does not serve Him yet.
Then let it begin with you.
Maybe nobody in your family understands your faith.
Maybe generations before you were marked by addiction, abuse, abandonment, rage, adultery, bitterness, or spiritual indifference.
But Jesus can transform what happens next.
Somebody has to become the person who says:
And maybe the first step is frighteningly simple.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
But sometimes publicly naming what your heart is surrendering becomes a moment you remember.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed tonight.
There will probably be a day when the decision becomes difficult again.
Not as a performance of spirituality.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of stewardship and partnership in that mission.
They may never walk into a church this week.
They may never message a pastor.
But they may stop long enough to read something you shared.
And God can use a simple act of faithfulness far beyond what you can see.
They are not purchasing spiritual status.

They are helping support the continued creation and distribution of Gospel-centered content while receiving deeper opportunities for biblical nourishment, discipleship, encouragement, accountability, and spiritual sharpening.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the Christian who has drifted.
Invite the seeker who still has questions.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Jesus could never want someone like them.
Because somewhere tonight, another person is standing at Shechem.
They may not call it Shechem.
They may call it their marriage.
“As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”
Now the words have reached you.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that you openly reject Jesus.
Perhaps it is that you keep postponing Him.
Today has been placed in your hands.
Christ is still calling sinners out of darkness.
Grace is still greater than your scandal.
The cross still announces forgiveness to everyone who comes to Christ in repentant faith.
And your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
And when the enemy whispers your old name, remember the Savior who walked into your scandal carrying a cross—and walked out of a tomb carrying your hope.
